result: Among 92 severe post-COVID patients, the 49% meeting CCC ME/CFS criteria had lower peak VO2 (13.0 vs 15.4 ml/kg/min, p=0.012), peak power (0.9 vs 1.1 W/kg) and O2 pulse (7.7 vs 8.5) than those without ME/CFS; 66% met objective work-disability thresholds and VO2 peak tracked Bell score and occupational status.
reason: Comparison is post-COVID ME/CFS vs post-COVID non-ME/CFS, not vs healthy controls, so it adds a post-COVID subgroup and disability link rather than replicating the case-control finding.

result: Within 92 severe long COVID patients, those meeting ME/CFS criteria had lower peak VO2 (13.0 vs 15.4 ml/kg/min), peak power and O2 pulse, and peak VO2 was lowest in those on sick leave (13.3) vs reintegration (16.0) or working (18.0).
reason: No recovered-control group, so it cannot replicate the LC-vs-control deficit; it adds an ME/CFS-subgroup and occupational-status gradient within LC.

result: In 12-25-year-old females followed 6 months after mild SARS-CoV-2, CyTOF found more hyperresponsive terminal NK cells, more activated/exhausted PD-1+ CD4 effector T cells and fewer marginal-zone and transitional B cells in both long COVID and fatigued uninfected controls, with no LC-specific immune change; terminal NK cells were the top machine-learning predictor of fatigue.
reason: Immune domain: a fatigue-general (not LC-specific) NK/T-cell signature with a fatigued-control comparison is not covered; immune-longcovid-overlap and immune-nk-cytotoxicity measure different things.

result: In 81 post-COVID syndrome patients, OCS-Plus deficits in delayed memory, attention and executive function showed no change over a median 4.4-month follow-up (all p>0.3, equivalence confirmed), unrelated to changes in depression or fatigue.
reason: Same cognitive domains in the long COVID version, adding time-course stability; screening tool and no control group limit weight.

result: In a college-student cohort, long COVID symptom burden fell between that of severe and moderate post-mononucleosis ME/CFS; no numbers given.
reason: Likely the already-cited Jason 2026 paper (same college mono cohort, 2026), and in any case it compares symptom burden rather than measuring post-mono CFS incidence; abstract is too thin.

result: Long COVID symptom burden fell between severe and moderate post-mononucleosis ME/CFS in a matched college cohort; no numbers given.
reason: Does not measure ME/CFS incidence after SARS-CoV-2; symptom-burden comparison with no quantitative results.

result: Meta-analysis of 17 RCTs (n=1944): exercise improved self-reported fatigue (SMD 0.85, I2 85%), QoL (SMD 0.99) and depression (0.56), but not cardiopulmonary function (SMD 0.13, 3 RCTs) or functional capacity (SMD 0.09, 4 RCTs); no difference in adverse events.
reason: Self-report gains without objective gains matches rather than contradicts the finding; pooled set likely includes PACE and does not address criteria or long-term follow-up, so extends not replicates.

result: Across 17 exercise RCTs (n=1944), self-reported fatigue and QoL improved but objective cardiopulmonary and functional capacity did not, and acceptability and adverse events did not differ between arms.
reason: Recovery rates are not measured; the no-difference-in-adverse-events result bears on the exercise-harms finding, though RCT adverse-event reporting is a weak test of PEM harm.

result: In 220 post-COVID clinic patients (Angers, 2020-2023), 26.4% had PEM, which was more frequent with 2020/2021 (pre-Omicron) infection (OR 5.68, 95% CI 1.66-19.45) and higher fatigue (OR 2.07).
reason: Measures PEM prevalence and its variant-era determinants in long COVID, not ME/CFS incidence after infection; retrospective record review.

result: In 60 ME/CFS patients vs 60 controls, reaction time on a 3D VR oculomotor task was slower at all disparities (1969 vs 1384 ms at 275 arcsec, p=0.0001; 1409 vs 1071 ms; 1126 vs 891 ms), and did not correlate with self-rated fatigue.
reason: Independent case-control cohort showing prolonged reaction time, same direction as the finding.
